questions.question: Which six-line Scots stanza form (rhyming 'aaabab') did Robert Burns popularize in 'To a Mouse' (1785) and 'To a Louse' (1786)?
questions.explanation: Burns mastered the six-line Standard Habbie stanza, rhyming aaabab with four tetrameter lines and two short dimeter lines.

questions.question: In Robert Burns's 'Tam o' Shanter' (1791), where does Tam see witches dancing, and which witch pulls off his mare Meg's tail?
options: Grasmere Parish Chapel; Old Martha Ray
Melrose Abbey Ruins; Gypsy Meg Merrilies
Alloway Kirk; Nannie in her 'cutty sark'
questions.explanation: In Burns's 1791 mock-heroic narrative, Tam watches witches dance in Alloway Kirk and flees Nannie across the Brig o' Doon.

questions.question: Which 1785 dramatic monologue by Robert Burns satirizes Calvinist hypocrisy and predestination through Elder William Fisher?
questions.explanation: Burns's 1785 monologue 'Holy Willie's Prayer' exposes the self-righteous hypocrisy of Calvinist church elder William Fisher.

questions.question: Which ornate 1780s–1790s poetic school led by Robert Merry and Hannah Cowley was demolished by William Gifford's 'The Baviad' (1791)?
questions.explanation: The Della Cruscans began with 'The Florence Miscellany' in 1785 and were crushed by William Gifford's 'The Baviad' and 'The Maeviad'.

questions.question: In William Blake's 'The Marriage of Heaven and Hell' (1790–1793), which section states 'The road of excess leads to the palace of wisdom'?
questions.explanation: Blake's 'The Marriage of Heaven and Hell' asserts 'Without Contraries is no progression' and includes the Proverbs of Hell.

questions.question: In William Blake's prophetic mythology ('The Book of Urizen', 1794), which figures personify oppressive Reason, Imagination, and Revolution?
questions.explanation: In Blake's private mythology, Urizen represents dogmatic reason, Los represents creative imagination, and Orc embodies revolution.

questions.question: In the Preface to which prophetic work (1804–1810) did William Blake include the famous hymn mentioning 'these dark Satanic Mills'?
questions.explanation: Blake's famous lyric 'And did those feet in ancient time', naming dark Satanic Mills, prefaces 'Milton: A Poem in Two Books'.

questions.question: Whose November 1789 sermon 'A Discourse on the Love of Our Country' directly provoked Edmund Burke's 'Reflections on the Revolution in France'?
questions.explanation: Dissenting minister Dr. Richard Price delivered 'A Discourse on the Love of Our Country' in November 1789, triggering Burke's 1790 reply.

questions.question: In 'Reflections on the Revolution in France' (1790), Edmund Burke lamented the fall of Marie Antoinette and warned against:
options: The enclosure of common village pastures by wealthy factory landlords
The passing of the age of chivalry and rule by 'a swinish multitude'
The arbitrary suspension of Habeas Corpus by Prime Minister Mr. Pitt
The tyranny of hereditary monarchs governing beyond the silent grave
questions.explanation: Burke mourned that the age of chivalry was gone and warned that learning would be trampled down by a swinish multitude.

questions.question: In Part I of 'Rights of Man' (1791), how did Thomas Paine famously criticize Edmund Burke's theatrical sympathy for French royalty?
options: 'He pities the plumage, but forgets the dying bird'
'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains'
'Inclosure came and trampled on labour's rights'
'Marriage is the worst of all legal monopolies'
questions.explanation: Paine wrote 'He pities the plumage, but forgets the dying bird' to expose Burke's indifference to the suffering French people.

questions.question: Before publishing 'A Vindication of the Rights of Woman' (1792), which work did Mary Wollstonecraft publish in November 1790 to answer Burke?
options: 'Letters Written in Sweden, Norway, and Denmark'
'A Vindication of the Rights of Men'
questions.explanation: Wollstonecraft published 'A Vindication of the Rights of Men' in November 1790 as the first major rebuttal to Burke's 'Reflections'.

questions.question: In 'A Vindication of the Rights of Woman' (1792, dedicated to Talleyrand), Mary Wollstonecraft attacked Book V of Rousseau's 'Emile' for:
options: Banning the study of botany, music, and domestic needlework in country schools
Educating the female character Sophie solely to be passive and pleasing to men
Rejecting companionate marriage in favour of monastic celibacy for young women
Advocating state-funded co-education for boys and girls in the French Republic
questions.explanation: Wollstonecraft critiqued Rousseau's 'Emile' and conduct writers Fordyce and Gregory for denying women rational education.

questions.question: In 'Political Justice' (1793), William Godwin's utilitarian 'Fire of Cambrai' dilemma argues that from a burning palace one must save:
options: Archbishop Fénelon rather than his chambermaid, even if the maid were one's mother
The royal library manuscripts rather than any living inhabitant inside the palace
One's own mother or sister first, because domestic affection outranks public utility
King Louis XVI rather than a peasant, to preserve the organic contract of the state
questions.explanation: Godwin argued that impartial universal benevolence requires saving Fénelon, author of 'Telemachus', over a chambermaid.

questions.question: In William Godwin's 1794 novel 'Things as They Are; or, The Adventures of Caleb Williams', which aristocratic master persecutes Caleb?
questions.explanation: In Godwin's 1794 novel, Squire Falkland uses the legal system to persecute his secretary Caleb Williams after Caleb discovers his secret murder.

questions.question: Which three reformist leaders of the London Corresponding Society were acquitted in Prime Minister Pitt's 1794 Treason Trials?
options: Leigh Hunt, his brother John Hunt, and William Hazlitt
Henry Orator Hunt, William Cobbett, and Richard Carlile
Robert Merry, William Gifford, and John Wilson Croker
Thomas Hardy, John Horne Tooke, and John Thelwall
questions.explanation: Defended by Thomas Erskine in 1794, Hardy, Tooke, and Thelwall were acquitted by London juries before Pitt passed the 1795 Gagging Acts.

questions.question: Which 1786 Oriental Gothic novel by William Beckford, subtitled 'An Arabian Tale', depicts a Caliph's descent into the Hall of Eblis?
questions.explanation: William Beckford's 1786 Oriental Gothic tale 'Vathek' portrays a Faustian quest ending in eternal torment in the Hall of Eblis.

questions.question: Ann Radcliffe used the 'explained supernatural' in 'The Mysteries of Udolpho' (1794) and 'The Italian' (1797), which feature which villains?
questions.explanation: Radcliffe's 'The Mysteries of Udolpho' features Emily St. Aubert and Montoni, while 'The Italian' features the sinister monk Schedoni.

questions.question: How did Matthew Gregory Lewis's 'The Monk' (1796), featuring the corrupt Capuchin abbot Ambrosio, depart from Ann Radcliffe's Gothic mode?
options: It rejected the explained supernatural for visceral horror and literal demons
It was composed entirely in Spenserian stanzas as an allegorical court romance
It explained all ghostly phenomena as harmless optical illusions of moonlight
It replaced medieval European castles with realistic English country-house life
questions.explanation: Unlike Radcliffe's sublime Terror and explained supernatural, Monk Lewis used graphic Horror and a literal demonic pact in 'The Monk'.

questions.question: In Book XI of 'The Prelude', how did William Wordsworth recall his youthful enthusiasm for the early French Revolution of 1789–1792?
options: 'The Sensual and the Dark rebel in vain, / Slaves by their own compulsion!'
'Whither is fled the visionary gleam? / Where is it now, the glory and the dream?'
'O Lady! we receive but what we give, / And in our life alone does Nature live'
'Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive, / But to be young was very heaven!'
questions.explanation: Wordsworth's 'The Prelude' famously captures early revolutionary rapture with Bliss was it in that dawn to be alive.

questions.question: In which 1798 poem, first printed in 'The Morning Post' as 'The Recantation', did Coleridge renounce France after its invasion of Switzerland?
questions.explanation: Coleridge published 'France: An Ode' in 1798 to recant his support for the French Republic after it invaded Switzerland.

questions.question: In Wordsworth's pastoral poem 'Michael' (1800), what remains unfinished at Green-head Ghyll after Michael's son Luke goes to the city?
questions.explanation: In Wordsworth's 1800 pastoral 'Michael', the ruined shepherd's stone sheepfold at Green-head Ghyll remains forever unfinished.

questions.question: When Wordsworth published 'The Excursion' in 1814, he announced it as the middle part of which vast, unfinished philosophical poem?
questions.explanation: Wordsworth planned 'The Recluse' as a three-part philosophical poem on Man, Nature, and Society, completing only 'The Prelude' and 'The Excursion'.

questions.question: In 'Biographia Literaria' (1817), how does Samuel Taylor Coleridge distinguish 'Imagination' from 'Fancy' and critique Wordsworth's Preface?
options: He agrees completely with Wordsworth that there is no difference between prose and verse diction
Imagination is a unifying creative power while Fancy combines fixities; rustic speech is flawed
Imagination belongs solely to natural scientists while Fancy belongs to rustic ballad singers
Fancy is the highest divine faculty of a poet while Primary Imagination is mechanical memory
questions.explanation: Coleridge divides Imagination into primary and secondary, contrasts it with mechanical Fancy, and critiques Wordsworth's theory of rustic diction.

questions.question: Which 1802 ode by Samuel Taylor Coleridge—originally drafted as a verse letter to Sara Hutchinson—mourns his fading 'shaping spirit of Imagination'?
options: 'Reflections on Having Left a Place of Retirement'
questions.explanation: Coleridge's 'Dejection: An Ode' of 1802 laments the loss of his joy and his shaping spirit of Imagination.

questions.question: Which editor of 'The Edinburgh Review' popularized the 'Lake School' label and began his 1814 review of 'The Excursion' with 'This will never do'?
questions.explanation: Whig editor Francis Jeffrey attacked the Lake School in 'The Edinburgh Review' and opened his 1814 review of 'The Excursion' with This will never do.

questions.question: Who wrote under the pseudonym 'Z' in 'Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine' (1817–1818) to attack Leigh Hunt, Keats, and Hazlitt as the 'Cockney School'?
questions.explanation: John Gibson Lockhart used the signature Z in 'Blackwood's Magazine' in October 1817 to launch the Cockney School attacks.

questions.question: In 'Cockney School of Poetry No. 4' (August 1818), how did Lockhart ('Z') mock John Keats's medical training after reviewing 'Endymion'?
options: 'Back to the shop Mr John, back to plasters, pills, and ointment boxes'
'Here lies a young London apothecary whose rhymes were writ in water'
'This will never do for the educated critical gentlemen of Edinburgh'
'A fiery particle very nearly snuffed out by a single quarterly article'
questions.explanation: Lockhart sneered at Keats's apothecary apprenticeship by telling him to go back to the shop, plasters, pills, and ointment boxes.

questions.question: In the Preface to which 1821 poem did Poet Laureate Robert Southey denounce Lord Byron and P. B. Shelley as the 'Satanic School'?
questions.explanation: In the March 1821 Preface to his hexameter poem 'A Vision of Judgement' on George III, Southey coined the term Satanic School.

questions.question: Where did Lord Byron publish his 1822 ottava rima parody 'The Vision of Judgment', in which Saint Peter knocks Southey into a lake?
options: In 'The Edinburgh Review', edited by Whig critic Francis Jeffrey and Sydney Smith
In 'The Quarterly Review', published in London by Byron's publisher John Murray
In the first issue of 'The Liberal', founded in Italy by Byron, Shelley, and Hunt
In 'Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine', edited by William Blackwood and John Wilson
questions.explanation: After John Murray feared prosecution, Byron published 'The Vision of Judgment' in October 1822 in the first issue of 'The Liberal'.

questions.question: On 27 February 1812, Lord Byron delivered his maiden speech in the House of Lords to oppose the Frame Breaking Bill targeting:
questions.explanation: Byron defended the desperate Luddite weavers against the 1812 Frame Breaking Act and wrote 'An Ode to the Framers of the Frame Bill'.

questions.question: Which 1817–1818 Venetian poem by Lord Byron marked his first use of the comic Italian 'ottava rima' stanza later perfected in 'Don Juan'?
questions.explanation: Byron's witty Venetian tale 'Beppo' introduced the ottava rima stanza that became the vehicle for 'Don Juan'.

questions.question: Which two philosophical dramatic poems by Lord Byron (1817 and 1821) portray an Alpine nobleman in the Alps and the first biblical murderer?
questions.explanation: Byron explored gloomy metaphysical rebellion in his dramatic poems 'Manfred' in 1817 and 'Cain: A Mystery' in 1821.

questions.question: In Shelley's 'The Masque of Anarchy' (written 1819 after Peterloo), which cabinet minister wears the mask of Murder before the call 'Ye are many—they are few'?
options: Whig Prime Minister Charles Earl Grey
questions.explanation: In 'The Masque of Anarchy', Shelley portrays Castlereagh as Murder, Eldon as Fraud, and Sidmouth as Hypocrisy.

questions.question: Which 1819 political sonnet by P. B. Shelley begins 'An old, mad, blind, despised, and dying King' and denounces 'liberticide' at Peterloo?
options: 'Feelings of a Republican on the Fall of Bonaparte'
questions.explanation: Shelley's sonnet 'England in 1819' attacks King George III, the Prince Regent, the Six Acts crisis, and the Peterloo Massacre.

questions.question: In 'Don Juan' (Canto XI), how did Lord Byron ironize the popular myth promoted in Shelley's 'Adonais' that hostile reviews killed John Keats?
options: That Keats drank 'a beaker full of the warm South and faded quietly into the forest dim'
That Keats's mind, 'that very fiery particle', let itself be 'snuff'd out by an article'
That Keats was 'a pale knight-at-arms loitering alone beside the withered autumn sedge'
That Keats was 'a starved London apothecary sent back to his plasters and ointment boxes'
questions.explanation: Byron quipped in 'Don Juan' that it was strange the mind, that very fiery particle, should let itself be snuffed out by an article.

questions.question: In John Keats's 'The Eve of St. Agnes' (1819, written in Spenserian stanzas), who are the two young lovers who elope into the storm?
questions.explanation: In Keats's 'The Eve of St. Agnes', Porphyro enters Madeline's chamber with old Angela's help and elopes with her into the storm.

questions.question: Which 1819 ballad by John Keats portrays a 'knight-at-arms, / Alone and palely loitering' after being enthralled by 'a faery's child'?
questions.explanation: Keats's 1819 ballad 'La Belle Dame sans Merci' depicts a pale knight abandoned on a cold hill's side where no birds sing.

questions.question: Which of John Keats's 1819 odes concludes with the lines "'Beauty is truth, truth beauty,'—that is all / Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know"?
questions.explanation: Keats's 'Ode on a Grecian Urn' of 1819 ends with the urn's famous message equating Beauty and Truth.

questions.question: In Jane Austen's 'Northanger Abbey' (1817), which heroine's overactive imagination is fuelled by reading Ann Radcliffe's 'The Mysteries of Udolpho'?
questions.explanation: In 'Northanger Abbey', Catherine Morland reads 'The Mysteries of Udolpho' and imagines gothic crimes at General Tilney's abbey.

questions.question: Jane Austen's 'Sense and Sensibility' (1811), contrasting the sisters Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, was first drafted in the 1790s under what title?
questions.explanation: Austen originally drafted 'Sense and Sensibility' in the 1790s under the title 'Elinor and Marianne'.

questions.question: In which 1818 Waverley novel by Sir Walter Scott does the humble Scottish heroine Jeanie Deans walk to London to save her sister Effie?
questions.explanation: Scott's 1818 novel 'The Heart of Midlothian' opens with the Edinburgh Porteous Riots and follows Jeanie Deans's journey to London.

questions.question: Along with Mary Shelley's 'Frankenstein' (1818), which 1819 prose tale by Dr. John Polidori grew out of the 1816 Villa Diodati ghost-story contest?
options: 'The Private Memoirs and Confessions of a Justified Sinner'
questions.explanation: Byron's physician John Polidori wrote 'The Vampyre' in 1819, introducing the aristocratic vampire Lord Ruthven, after the 1816 Villa Diodati summer.

questions.question: In Mary Shelley's 'Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus' (1818), which Arctic explorer narrates the outer epistolary frame to his sister?
questions.explanation: Arctic sea captain Robert Walton rescues Victor Frankenstein on the ice and frames the novel in letters to his sister Margaret Saville.

questions.question: Which 1820 Gothic novel by Charles Robert Maturin uses nested frame tales to trace an ancestor who bargains his soul for 150 extra years of life?
questions.explanation: Charles Robert Maturin's 'Melmoth the Wanderer' of 1820 employs a Chinese-box frame structure to recount a Faustian curse.

questions.question: Which 1818 satirical novel by Thomas Love Peacock parodies Shelley as Scythrop Glowry, Byron as Mr. Cypress, and Coleridge as Mr. Flosky?
questions.explanation: Thomas Love Peacock's 1818 conversation novel 'Nightmare Abbey' satirizes Romantic melancholy through Scythrop, Cypress, and Flosky.

questions.question: Which essay in Charles Lamb's 'Essays of Elia' (1823) ends with the revelation that his listeners, Alice and John, are merely 'nothing, less than nothing, and dreams'?
questions.explanation: Lamb's 'Dream Children: A Reverie' poignantly imagines the children he might have had with Alice W—n before waking alone.

questions.question: In which 1825 collection of contemporary portraits did William Hazlitt call Coleridge 'the most impressive talker of his age'?
questions.explanation: William Hazlitt's 'The Spirit of the Age' of 1825 profiles leading Romantic writers including Coleridge, Wordsworth, Byron, and Scott.

questions.question: Which two famous critical and ironic essays were written by Thomas De Quincey in 1823 and 1827 respectively?
options: 'A Defence of Poetry' and 'The Necessity of Atheism'
'On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth' and 'On Murder Considered as One of the Fine Arts'
'My First Acquaintance with Poets' and 'On Going a Journey'
'Dream Children: A Reverie' and 'A Dissertation upon Roast Pig'
questions.explanation: De Quincey wrote 'On the Knocking at the Gate in Macbeth' in 1823 and 'On Murder Considered as One of the Fine Arts' in 1827.

questions.question: Which 'Peasant Poet' of Helpston ('The Shepherd's Calendar', 1827) mourned Parliamentary Enclosures with 'Inclosure came and trampled on the grave / Of labour's rights'?
questions.explanation: John Clare, the Northamptonshire Peasant Poet, chronicled the destruction of rural common lands by Enclosure Acts.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the periodicals and political landmarks of the Romantic Period (1785–1832) is NOT correct?
options: The First Reform Act of 1832 granted immediate universal suffrage to all adult men and women
'The Examiner' (founded 1808) was a radical liberal paper edited by Leigh Hunt and John Hunt
'The Edinburgh Review' (founded 1802) was a Whig quarterly edited for years by Francis Jeffrey
'The Quarterly Review' (founded 1809) was established by Tories including Scott and John Murray
questions.explanation: The First Reform Act of 1832 abolished rotten boroughs and widened the franchise, but still restricted voting to a minority of men.
